question: What did you like most about this prompt?
answer: The machine section and the hub. The brief names exact versions, flags, what this computer lacks and the stand-ins to use, so I could prototype the exact stack here instead of guessing, and hand the builders recipes that were actually run. The hub protocol comes with a real harness, so I could test the multiplayer design against the checks the hub itself runs before writing it down. I also liked the balance: firm where it matters (tech stack, 10-foot UX, dev mode, attract mode, single file) and open where the design should live (genre, perspective, research, effort).

question: What was confusing?
answer: Six things. 1) "Follow the hub for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own" could mean the game must simply keep working outside a session, or must also have its own multiplayer there. The hub's check script uses "on its own" for the page opened outside a session, so I specified that and added couch co-op to cover the other reading. 2) The WebGPU flags in the machine notes lost the device right after the first frame here, and the note that a WebGPU canvas "can come out blank" reads as a harmless quirk when it was really that failure. Adding --use-vulkan=swiftshader and --use-angle=swiftshader, from the hub's own script, fixed it, and screenshots then worked. 3) "Capture its world, characters, themes and tone" sits next to "build an original game". I kept archetypes, structure and tone, with every name and character new, but I was inferring that line. 4) "Title/menu screen" for attract mode doesn't say which screens count. I included Title, Main Menu and Free Play, and left out reading screens such as Settings and About. 5) TASK.md speaks to the builder, so I had to work out which parts bind a planner and which only describe what builders must do. 6) "Leave out TASK.md's file and folder names" doesn't say whether that includes the exit interview file. I left it out too.

question: What was the hardest thing to do?
answer: Moving a pointer-and-motion game onto two sticks and a TV without losing its feel, when nothing here can feel it. There's no real controller and no human player, so tracing a cut with a thumbstick, the pull tolerance and the aim assist are reasoned numbers, not playtested ones. I can't vouch for them, so I gave builders live sliders and bot-based invariants to tune with, and said which recipes were verified. Next hardest was the plan's depth: it had to be complete enough to build from without me, for builders whose capability and budget I don't know, without burying them. That's why it has a build order and a stated cut order. It's still long, about 16,000 words, and I can't tell from here whether that's the right size. Being strict about what "verified" means was harder than I expected, too: a render-target portrait ran without errors on both backends and was still upside down, and only a test with colored markers caught it.

question: What would you change in this prompt?
answer: 1) Correct the WebGPU flags in the machine notes to the five that work, and drop or explain the blank-screenshot note. 2) Warn that python3 -m http.server buffers its output when piped, so a script waiting for the port line hangs (that hung my first harness run until its timeout), or suggest python3 -u or a small Node server. 3) Say outright whether multiplayer outside the hub is required, and whether a session mode is preferred. 4) State how close to the source's world and characters is acceptable, for example archetypes yes, names no. 5) Define which screens count as title/menu for attract mode. 6) Give the planner a short section of its own: who the builders are (the range of models and effort levels), what budget they have, and what else they will see, so the plan can be sized on purpose instead of by guess.
